## Everything Has a Cost

You have one free hour. You can see friends, finish a project, or sleep. Whatever you pick, you did not do the other two.

That sentence is most of economics.

Economics is often described as being about money. It is really about **scarcity**: there is not enough of something to satisfy every want, so choosing is unavoidable. Time is scarce. Money is scarce. Clean water is scarce in some places and not in others. Even attention is scarce.

Scarcity is not the same as being rare, and it is not the same as being expensive. Something is **scarce** when people want more of it than exists. Sand is cheap and enormously common, and construction sand is genuinely scarce in some regions because demand outruns what can be dug.

Because things are scarce, every choice is a **trade-off**. You gain one thing and give up another.

Economists give the thing you gave up a name: **opportunity** cost. It is not everything you turned down. It is the single **alternative** you would have picked instead — your next best option. If you chose sleep over friends and a project, and you would have chosen friends next, then the opportunity cost of sleeping is seeing your friends. The project does not count. It was third.

That definition sounds fussy and it is the useful part. It forces you to name one specific thing rather than waving at everything.

Opportunity cost also explains decisions that look strange from outside. A town that spends on a new road is not against libraries. It made a choice, and the library was what it gave up. Judging the decision means comparing the **benefit** of the road against the library, not against nothing.

There is a trap worth knowing. Money already spent and not recoverable is a **sunk** cost, and it should not affect what you do next. If you paid for a ticket to a film you now know you will hate, the money is gone whether you go or not. The real choice is only about the next two hours. People find this genuinely hard, and knowing the word does not make it easy.

One more idea. Doing a bit more of something is a **marginal** decision. The question is rarely all or nothing. It is: is one more hour of practice worth what that hour costs me?

So when you meet a decision, yours or a government's, ask two things. What is scarce here? And what exactly got given up?

## Everything Has a Cost

You have one free hour. Suppose you can spend it on one of three mutually exclusive plans: see friends, work on a project, or rest. Choosing one prevents those same minutes from being used for another plan.

**Scarcity** means available resources cannot satisfy all the competing wants for them. It concerns time, money, materials, space and attention, not just rare or expensive objects. Whether a resource is scarce for a particular activity depends on what is available, where and when it is available, and how much is wanted. A free price does not guarantee unlimited availability.

A **choice** selects among feasible alternatives. A **trade-off** describes giving up one benefit or use to obtain another. Some choices allow combinations; our one-hour example rules them out so the comparison is clear.

**Opportunity cost** is the value of the next-best feasible alternative forgone. If you choose rest and seeing friends is your next-best option, the cost is the benefit you would have received from seeing friends during that hour. Do not add every lower-ranked option. If an alternative is a feasible combination of activities, evaluate that whole alternative rather than insisting it must be a single named activity.

Suppose a fictional town has a fixed budget and only two feasible, mutually exclusive proposals: a road or a library. If it chooses the road, the forgone library benefit is the opportunity cost. A real town may have many alternatives; you cannot assume the runner-up without examining them.

A **benefit** is an expected gain. Compare future benefits and costs using stated assumptions, including effects that are hard to express in money. Different people may rank options differently.

A **sunk cost** is a past cost that cannot be recovered. Suppose a film ticket cannot be refunded, resold or transferred. The purchase money is gone whichever activity you choose now. That past payment alone should not justify attending a film you no longer want to see. The remaining time, travel cost and expected experience still matter. If a refund or resale is possible, that recoverable value is relevant.

Past training time cannot be recovered, but the skills you gained can affect future choices. Likewise, already-owned equipment may have future use or resale value. Do not confuse a sunk purchase cost with an asset's remaining value.

A **marginal** decision compares an additional benefit with an additional cost: is one more hour of practice worth what that hour displaces? An **incentive** changes a choice's expected benefit or cost. It can influence choices without forcing everyone to respond the same way.

In the community-room task, one room is available from four to five and four groups want the entire slot. Rank the feasible uses, explain your criteria, identify the next-best forgone benefit, and distinguish unrecoverable past spending from consequences that remain ahead.

The sort's scenarios are fictional and include explicit assumptions. “Available for this use” does not mean the resource is unlimited everywhere. Classify the highlighted resource or past expenditure in its stated context.
